note: There were no continuous front lines in this war: shaded areas show who held which ground, and arrows show the main campaigns. Outlines are approximate, and armies often held little more than the towns and roads they garrisoned.

chapters.title: The Bohemian revolt
chapters.text: After the Defenestration of Prague in May 1618, Bohemia's Protestant nobles set up their own government and raised an army. Ernst von Mansfeld stormed loyal Catholic Pilsen in November, and in 1619 the revolt spread through Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia while Count Thurn's army reached the walls of Vienna in June. But Budweis held out for Ferdinand, whose general Bucquoy beat Mansfeld at Sablat on 10 June. In August the rebels deposed Ferdinand and chose Frederick V of the Palatinate as their king.

chapters.title: White Mountain
arrows: Imperial and Catholic League armies invade Bohemia
chapters.text: Frederick's support melted away in 1620. Lutheran Saxony sided with Ferdinand in return for Lusatia and occupied it, while an imperial and Catholic League army paid for by Maximilian of Bavaria marched into southern Bohemia. On 8 November it routed the Bohemian army on the White Mountain outside Prague in about an hour, entered the city the next day, and Frederick fled. Protestant forces in Silesia and Moravia fought on for a while, but Bohemia was lost.

chapters.title: The Palatinate overrun
arrows: Tilly's Catholic League army enters the Palatinate
chapters.text: While Frederick lost Bohemia, Spain's Army of Flanders under Spinola invaded his own lands on the Rhine in August 1620, taking Kreuznach and Oppenheim in September. In 1622 Frederick's allies won at Mingolsheim but were beaten at Wimpfen and Höchst, and Tilly and Córdoba besieged the English-garrisoned towns one by one: Heidelberg fell on 19 September and Mannheim on 2 November. Frankenthal surrendered in March 1623, and Frederick's electoral title went to Maximilian of Bavaria.

chapters.title: Denmark's war: Lutter to Lübeck
arrows: Mansfeld attacks Wallenstein's bridgehead at Dessau
Christian IV advances south, then falls back on Lutter
Tilly and Wallenstein overrun Holstein and Jutland
chapters.text: Christian IV of Denmark, also Duke of Holstein, entered the war in 1625 to lead the Protestants of northern Germany. In 1626 Wallenstein's new imperial army beat Mansfeld at the Dessau Bridge and Tilly crushed Christian at Lutter on 27 August. By the end of 1627 the two generals had occupied Mecklenburg, Pomerania and Jutland as far as the Limfjord, but Stralsund held out against Wallenstein's siege in 1628. The Treaty of Lübeck in 1629 gave Denmark back its lands in return for leaving the war.

chapters.title: Gustavus Adolphus lands
arrows: Gustavus Adolphus lands and takes Stettin
Gustavus moves up the Oder to Frankfurt
chapters.text: In the summer of 1630 King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed at Peenemünde in Pomerania with some 18,000 men and took Stettin, the Pomeranian capital, within weeks. For the rest of 1630 the Swedes secured the Oder estuary, then moved up the river and stormed Frankfurt an der Oder in April 1631. They could not save Magdeburg, which had declared for Sweden: Tilly's army stormed it on 20 May 1631 and some 20,000 people died as the city burned.

chapters.title: Breitenfeld and the march to the Rhine
arrows: Gustavus marches through Thuringia to the Main and Rhine
Gustavus invades Bavaria: Donauwörth, Rain and Munich
chapters.text: When Tilly invaded Saxony, its elector joined Sweden, and on 17 September 1631 their armies routed Tilly at Breitenfeld near Leipzig. Gustavus swept through Thuringia to Würzburg, Frankfurt and Mainz by the winter, while the Saxons occupied Prague. In spring 1632 he took Nuremberg and Donauwörth, forced the Lech at Rain, where Tilly was mortally wounded, and entered Munich on 17 May, though Ingolstadt held out.

chapters.title: Wallenstein and Lützen
chapters.text: The emperor recalled Wallenstein, who drove the Saxons out of Bohemia and then faced Gustavus at Nuremberg, where the Swedish assault on his entrenched camp at the Alte Veste failed in September. Wallenstein then invaded Saxony and took Leipzig in early November. Gustavus followed and attacked him at Lützen on 16 November; the Swedes held the field and Wallenstein withdrew into Bohemia, but Gustavus himself was killed.

chapters.title: Nördlingen and the Peace of Prague
arrows: Ferdinand of Hungary takes Regensburg and marches up the Danube
The Cardinal-Infante's Spanish army joins him
Horn and Bernard march to relieve Nördlingen
chapters.text: In 1634 the emperor's son Ferdinand of Hungary retook Swedish-held Regensburg on 26 July, marched up the Danube and besieged Nördlingen. A Spanish army under the Cardinal-Infante joined him, and on 6 September they destroyed the Swedish army of Horn and Bernard of Saxe-Weimar. Swedish power in southern Germany collapsed: the imperial army retook most of Württemberg, and in May 1635 Saxony and most German princes made peace with the emperor at Prague.

chapters.title: France against Spain: Corbie to Rocroi
chapters.text: Catholic France declared war on Spain in May 1635 to stop the Habsburgs winning. In July 1636 a Spanish and imperial army from the Spanish Netherlands took La Capelle and Le Catelet, crossed the Somme and captured Corbie on 15 August, causing panic in Paris, but the French besieged the town and won it back in November. In May 1643 a Spanish army besieging Rocroi was crushed by the young Duke of Enghien.

chapters.title: Breisach and the Upper Rhine
arrows: Bernard of Saxe-Weimar crosses the Rhine at Rheinfelden
Bernard marches down the Rhine to Breisach
chapters.text: France paid Bernard of Saxe-Weimar's army to fight on the Rhine. In early 1638 he crossed the river at Rheinfelden and, after losing a first battle there, defeated and captured the imperial generals Werth and Savelli on 3 March. He went on to take Rheinfelden and Freiburg, then besieged Breisach, the great Habsburg fortress on the Rhine, which surrendered on 17 December. With Breisach and Alsace in French hands, Spain could no longer send troops overland from Italy to the Netherlands.

chapters.title: Jankau and the march on Vienna
chapters.text: In 1645 the Swedish general Lennart Torstensson invaded Bohemia and destroyed the main imperial army at Jankau on 6 March. His army marched through Moravia to the Danube opposite Vienna, but could not cross the river or besiege so large a city. He besieged Brno instead from May to August, where a small garrison held out while disease and hunger cost the besiegers over 8,000 men, and by the following February the Swedes had been driven out of Bohemia.

chapters.title: The last campaigns and the Peace of Westphalia
arrows: Piccolomini drives the invaders out of Bavaria
chapters.text: With peace talks under way in Westphalia, the armies fought on. A Swedish and French army beat the last imperial-Bavarian army at Zusmarshausen on 17 May 1648 and plundered Bavaria as far as the Isar, until Piccolomini manoeuvred it back across the Lech by October. In July a Swedish column seized Prague Castle and the Lesser Town, but not the Old Town. The Peace of Westphalia was signed on 24 October, giving Sweden western Pomerania and Bremen-Verden and France parts of Alsace.
